papers.title: Review of Superconducting Qubit Devices and Their Large-Scale Integration
papers.abstract: The superconducting qubit quantum computer is one of the most promising quantum computing architectures for large-scale integration due to its maturity and close proximity to the well-established semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure. From an education perspective, it also bridges classical microwave electronics and quantum electrodynamics. In this paper, we will review the basics of quantum computers, superconductivity, and Josephson junctions. We then introduce important technologies and concepts related to DiVincenzo's criteria, which are the necessary conditions for the superconducting qubits to work as a useful quantum computer. Firstly, we will discuss various types of superconducting qubits formed with Josephson junctions, from which we will understand the trade-off across multiple design parameters, including their noise immunity. Secondly, we will discuss different schemes to achieve entanglement gate operations, which are a major bottleneck in achieving more efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing. Thirdly, we will review readout engineering, including the implementations of the Purcell filters and quantum-limited amplifiers. Finally, we will discuss the nature and review the studies of two-level system defects, which are currently the limiting factor of qubit coherence time. DiVincenzo's criteria are only the necessary conditions for a technology to be eligible for quantum computing. To have a useful quantum computer, large-scale integration is required. We will review proposals and developments for the large-scale integration of superconducting qubit devices. By comparing with the application of electronic design automation (EDA) in semiconductors, we will also review the use of EDA in superconducting qubit quantum computer design, which is necessary for its large-scale integration.

similar_to.title: A Quantum Engineer's Guide to Superconducting Qubits
Superconducting Qubits: Current State of Play

summary.summary: This review covers superconducting qubit design principles, implementations of DiVincenzo's criteria (qubit types, two-photon gates, readout with Purcell filters and quantum-limited amplifiers, and two-level system defects), and pathways to large-scale integration. The paper emphasizes the role of electronic design automation and scalable architecture in advancing superconducting quantum computers beyond single-device demonstrations.
summary.motivation: Superconducting qubits are a mature platform with proximity to established semiconductor fabrication, but achieving fault-tolerant quantum computers requires systematic understanding of design trade-offs and industrial-scale integration methodologies.
summary.method: Comprehensive review of Josephson junction-based qubit types, gate operation schemes, readout engineering techniques including Purcell filtering, two-level system physics limiting coherence, and application of EDA tools to circuit design for scalability.
summary.result: The paper identifies two-level system defects as the primary coherence bottleneck and proposes that EDA-driven design automation, adapted from semiconductor industry, is necessary for scaling beyond tens of qubits to practical quantum computers.

papers.title: Detailed, interpretable characterization of mid-circuit measurement on a transmon qubit
papers.abstract: Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) are critical components of the quantum error correction protocols expected to enable utility-scale quantum computing. MCMs can be modeled by quantum instruments (a type of quantum operation or process), which can be characterized self-consistently using gate set tomography. However, experimentally estimated quantum instruments are often hard to interpret or relate to device physics. We address this challenge by adapting the error generator formalism -- previously used to interpret noisy quantum gates by decomposing their error processes into physically meaningful sums of "elementary errors" -- to MCMs. We deploy our new analysis on a transmon qubit device to tease out and quantify error mechanisms including amplitude damping, readout error, and imperfect collapse. We examine in detail how the magnitudes of these errors vary with the readout pulse amplitude, recover the key features of dispersive readout predicted by theory, and show that these features can be modeled parsimoniously using a reduced model with just a few parameters.

similar_to.title: Model-based Optimization of Superconducting Qubit Readout

summary.summary: The paper extends the error generator formalism to mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) on superconducting qubits by modeling MCM errors using a circuit gadget representation and decomposing quantum instruments into physically interpretable elementary deviations. Gate set tomography characterization of a transmon dispersive readout reveals amplitude damping ($T_1$ effects), readout error, imperfect collapse (weakness), and AC Stark shift-induced non-Markovianity, with errors quantified as functions of readout pulse amplitude across $V = 0$ to $1.8 \times V_0$.
summary.motivation: Quantum error correction requires high-fidelity MCMs, but their errors are difficult to interpret from estimated quantum instruments. While error generators have successfully decomposed gate errors into physical mechanisms, no analogous framework existed for MCMs, limiting diagnostic capabilities for measurement debugging and mitigation.
summary.method: The authors adapted error generators to MCMs by constructing a two-qubit gadget (CNOT with virtual qubit) that represents an MCM, enabling the extraction of 28 first-order MCM-gauge-invariant (FOMGI) quantities via gate set tomography on a transmon with $\chi_{01}/2\pi = -0.26$ MHz and $\kappa/2\pi = 0.16$ MHz, swept across readout amplitudes with $N = 8 \times 10^3$ to $4 \times 10^4$ shots per circuit.
summary.result: Pre-MCM amplitude damping increases with readout amplitude while post-MCM decay remains constant, pure readout error and weakness dominate below $V = 0.6 \times V_0$, and a measure-and-prepare model with one additional AC Stark shift parameter achieves $N_\sigma < 2$ model violation at the nominal amplitude, reducing required parameters from 28 to 43 without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Enabling large-scale digital quantum simulations with superconducting qubits
papers.abstract: Quantum computing promises to revolutionize several scientific and technological domains through fundamentally new ways of processing information. Among its most compelling applications is digital quantum simulation, where quantum computers are used to replicate the behavior of other quantum systems. This could enable the study of problems that are otherwise intractable on classical computers, transforming fields such as quantum chemistry, condensed matter physics, and materials science. Despite this potential, realizations of practical quantum advantage for relevant problems are hindered by imperfections of current devices. This also affects quantum hardware based on superconducting circuits which is among the most advanced and scalable platforms. The envisaged long-term solution of fault-tolerant quantum computers that correct their own errors remains out of reach mainly due to the associated qubit number overhead. As a result, the field has developed strategies that combine quantum and classical resources, exploit hardware-native operations, and employ error mitigation techniques to extract meaningful results from noisy data. This doctoral thesis contributes to this broader effort by exploring methods for advancing quantum simulation across the full computational stack, including hardware-level innovations, refined techniques for noise modeling and error mitigation, and algorithmic improvements enabled by efficient measurement processing.

summary.summary: This doctoral thesis develops methods to advance digital quantum simulation on superconducting qubits through hardware innovations, noise modeling, error mitigation, and algorithmic improvements across the full computational stack. The work addresses the fundamental challenge that current noisy devices cannot yet achieve fault-tolerant operation, requiring hybrid quantum-classical strategies to extract meaningful results.
summary.motivation: Practical quantum advantage for scientifically relevant problems remains hindered by device imperfections in superconducting qubit platforms, and fault-tolerant approaches require prohibitive qubit overhead.
summary.method: The thesis explores coordinated improvements at multiple levels: hardware-level innovations, refined noise characterization and error mitigation techniques, and algorithmic enhancements exploiting efficient measurement processing and hardware-native operations.
summary.result: The thesis contributes to enabling quantum simulation on near-term superconducting devices through combined strategies that merge quantum and classical resources to extract meaningful results from noisy data.
